structure.title: Differential genome-wide associated variants and enriched pathways of ECG parameters among people with versus without HIV
structure.summary: The partial document discusses a study that investigates the genetic variants and pathways associated with electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters among people with HIV (PWH) compared to HIV-negative controls. The study aims to understand how the host genome influences ECG abnormalities, which are more prevalent in PWH. It presents findings from a genome-wide association study (GWAS) involving 1,730 PWH and 3,746 HIV-negative individuals, identifying 18 novel genetic variants linked to ECG parameters such as PR interval, QRS duration, and QTc interval. The results indicate significant interactions between genetic variants and HIV infection, suggesting that the host genome may affect cardiac electrical activity in the context of HIV. The study highlights the distinct genetic influences on ECG parameters in PWH, emphasizing the need to explore the interplay between host genetics and HIV infection in understanding cardiovascular risks in this population.

Differential genome-wide associated variants and
enriched pathways of ECG parameters among people
with versus without HIV
Jiayu Hea,b,c, M, Yingying Dinga,b,M, Haijiang Lina,d, Xing Liua,b,
Xiaoxiao Chena,d, Weiwei Shend, Sujuan Zhoua,b,c, Cheng Fenga,b,
Miaochen Wanga,b, Jingjing Xiaa,band Na Hea,b,c
Objectives: People with HIV (PWH) are more likely to develop ECG abnormalities.
Substantial evidence exists for genetic contribution to ECG parameters among generalpopulation. However, whether and how would host genome associate with ECGparameters among PWH is unclear. Our research aims to analyze and compare geneticvariants, mapped genes, and enriched pathways of ECG parameters among PWH andHIV-negative controls.
Design: A cross-sectional study.
Method: We performed a large original genome-wide association study (GWAS) of
ECG parameters among PWH ( n¼1730) and HIV-negative controls ( n¼3746).
Genome-wide interaction analyses were also conducted.
Results: A total of 18 novel variants were detected among PWH, six for PR interval
including rs76345397 at ATL2 , 11 for QRS duration including rs10483994 at
KCNK10 and rs2478830 at JCAD , and one for QTc interval (rs9815364). Among
HIV-negative controls, we identiﬁed vari ants located at previously reported ECG-
related genes ( SCN5A ,CNOT1 ). Genetic variants had a signiﬁcant interaction with
HIV infection ( P<5/C210
/C08), implying that HIV infection and host genome might
jointly inﬂuence ECG parameters. Mapped genes for PR interval and QRS duration
among PWH were enriched in the biological process of viral genome replication and
host response to virus, respectively, whereas enriched pathways for PR intervalamong HIV-negative controls were in the cellular component of voltage-gatedsodium channel complex.
Conclusion: The present GWAS indicated a distinctive impact of host genome on
quantitative ECG parameters among PWH. Different from HIV-negative controls, hostgenome might inﬂuence the cardiac electrical activity by interfering with HIV viralinfection, production, and latency among PWH.

Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has superbly improved the
prognosis of people with HIV (PWH). As a consequence,

Previous studies have indicated thatPWH are more likely to develop cardiac complications,including atherosclerosis, arrhythmia, myocardial infarc-tion, sudden cardiac death, and heart failure whencompared with HIV-negative controls [2,3].
ECG is valuable and reliable in cardiovascular assessment
and an essential tool for arrhythmia and various cardiac
disorders diagnosis [4]. The measurements routinely
obtained with ECG include PR interval, QRS duration,and QT interval, which are indicative of the function ofthe conduction system and provide important prognosticinformation [5]. The QTinterval reﬂects myocardial repolarization and is a risk

death [8]. Studies have shown that the prevalence of ECGabnormalities was higher among PWH compared withgeneral population, but mechanisms behind them werestill unclear [1].

SCN5A, CNOT1, KCNQ1 genes were associated with
PR interval, QRS duration, or QT interval among thegeneral population [12–15]. However, genetic associationstudy on ECG parameters among PWH was lacking. analyses. Uncovering the genetic architecture of ECGparameters among PWH can help dissect pathogenicmechanism and development of arrhythmia and other

The partial document discusses a genome-wide association study (GWA) analyzing the relationship between electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters and genetic variants in individuals with and without HIV. It outlines the statistical methods used, including linear mixed models (LMM) and generalized linear mixed models (GLMM), to account for population stratification and relatedness. The document details the significance thresholds for genetic associations and describes the statistical analyses performed, including comparisons of baseline characteristics based on HIV serostatus and the interaction between HIV infection and genetic variants on ECG parameters.

The results section presents demographic and ECG characteristics of the study participants, highlighting differences in ECG parameters between people with HIV (PWH) and HIV-negative individuals. It notes significant associations between HIV infection and various ECG parameters, as well as the impact of hypertension on these parameters. The document also reports on genetic variants associated with ECG parameters, identifying specific single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that reached genome-wide significance for PR interval and QRS duration among PWH, while different variants were significant in HIV-negative controls. Overall, the study aims to elucidate the genetic factors influencing ECG abnormalities in the context of HIV infection.

Additionally, the document includes visual representations of the data, such as Manhattan plots and Circos plots, to illustrate the findings.

nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses the findings of a study that mapped genetic variants associated with electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters, specifically PR interval, QRS duration, and QTc interval, in a cohort of over 5,300 individuals, including people living with HIV (PWH) and HIV-negative controls. Key points include:

1. **eQTL Mapping**: The gene ITGA9 was identified through expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping, with significant associations found in both PWH and controls.

2. **Significant Gene Sets**: Among PWH, significant gene sets related to PR interval were linked to viral genome replication and DNA cytosine deamination, while QRS duration was associated with responses to viral infections. In HIV-negative controls, the PR interval was linked to voltage-gated sodium channel complexes.

3. **Genome-Wide Significant Variants**: The study identified 18 genome-wide significant variants in PWH, with specific variants associated with PR interval (6), QRS duration (11), and QTc interval (1). Notable genes included SCN5A and CNOT1, previously linked to ECG abnormalities.

4. **Biological Processes**: The mapped genes for PR interval in PWH were enriched in processes related to viral replication and DNA deamination, while QRS duration was associated with responses to viruses and lipid catabolism.

5. **Specific Gene Associations**: Variants at ATL2 and ENTHD1 were linked to PR interval, with ATL2 implicated in HIV-related neurodegenerative diseases and viral replication. Variants at KCNK10 and JCAD were associated with QRS duration, with KCNK10 linked to heart failure and arrhythmia.

6. **QTc Interval Variant**: A significant variant at RNF13 was found to influence ER stress-induced apoptosis, potentially affecting cardiac electrical activity in the context of HIV.

7. **HIV Interaction**: The study highlights the interaction between HIV infection and genetic variants affecting ECG parameters, suggesting that HIV may significantly influence cardiac electrical activity and gene expression.

8. **Future Research**: The document concludes that further investigation is needed to understand the mechanisms by which HIV integration affects host gene expression and its implications for ECG parameters in PWH compared to HIV-negative individuals.

structure.summary: The partial document discusses a genome-wide association study (GWAS) that investigates the impact of host genetic variants on electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters among people with HIV (PWH) compared to HIV-negative controls. Key findings include the role of specific genes, such as APOBEC3A and SCN5A, in influencing HIV latency and cardiac electrical activity. The study highlights that the host genome may affect ECG parameters by interacting with HIV viral activities, suggesting a unique relationship between HIV infection and cardiac conduction. Limitations of the study include the lack of replication due to difficulties in finding additional cohorts and the absence of SNP genotype imputation. The document concludes that understanding the genetic and biological pathways involved could provide insights into conduction abnormalities in PWH. The study was approved by an institutional review board and supported by various funding sources.

impact of higher ECG abnormality prevalence among
HIV-negative controls on genetic association analyses alsowarrants further exploration.

nodes.summary:
The partial document primarily discusses various studies related to electrocardiographic parameters, genetic associations, and cardiovascular health. Key points include:

1. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identifying associations with PR interval, QTc interval, and QRS duration, highlighting genetic factors influencing these electrocardiographic traits.
2. The prognostic significance of electrocardiographic measurements in predicting cardiovascular outcomes, including cardiovascular death and arrhythmic risk.
3. Research on familial aggregation and heritability of electrocardiographic intervals, emphasizing the genetic basis of heart rate variability and conduction disorders.
4. The role of specific genetic variants, such as those in the SCN5A and KCNQ1 genes, in cardiac conduction diseases and their implications for arrhythmias.
5. Studies exploring the interactions between HIV infection and cardiovascular health, including the impact of HIV on carotid artery thickness and genetic variants associated with subclinical atherosclerosis.
6. The application of mixed-model association methods and tools for analyzing complex traits in large datasets, facilitating the understanding of genetic influences on cardiovascular and other health-related traits.

Overall, the document synthesizes findings from multiple studies that connect genetic factors to electrocardiographic traits and cardiovascular risk, with a focus on both general populations and specific groups such as those with HIV.

nodes.title: Genetic variants associated with ECG parameters
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses a genome-wide association study (GWAS) that investigates the impact of host genetic variants on electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters among people with HIV (PWH) and HIV-negative controls. It highlights the role of specific genes, such as APOBEC3A and SCN5A, in influencing cardiac electrical activity and the potential interaction between HIV infection and genetic factors affecting ECG metrics. The study identifies differences in genetic associations between PWH and controls, suggesting that the host genome may modulate cardiac conduction through mechanisms related to HIV viral activity. Limitations of the study, including the lack of replication and SNP genotype imputation, are acknowledged. The findings aim to enhance understanding of the biological pathways involved in cardiac conduction abnormalities in PWH, with implications for future research and validation of candidate genetic variants.

false discovery rate and candidate SNPs and genes werepresented for future validation. However, all the association results were basedon the actual measurement of genetic variants, which maymake sure the authenticity of GWA analyses. Lastly, the
impact of higher ECG abnormality prevalence among
HIV-negative controls on genetic association analyses alsowarrants further exploration.

The present GWAS indicated a distinctive impact of hostgenome on quantitative ECG parameters among PWH,as well as signiﬁcant interaction effects between HIVinfection and genetic variants on ECG parameters.Different from HIV-negative controls, host genome
might inﬂuence the cardiac electrical activity by
interfering HIV viral infection, production, and latencyamong PWH. Better understanding of the biologicpathways and molecular genetics associated with cardiacconduction may offer insight into the pathogenesis ofconduction abnormalities among PWH.Acknowledgements

structure.title: Conclusion
structure.summary: The partial document discusses a genome-wide association study (GWAS) that investigates the impact of host genetic variants on electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters among people with HIV (PWH) compared to HIV-negative controls. Key findings include the role of specific genes, such as APOBEC3A and SCN5A, in influencing HIV latency and cardiac electrical activity. The study highlights differences in genetic associations affecting ECG parameters between PWH and controls, suggesting that the host genome may modulate cardiac function through interactions with HIV viral activities. Limitations of the study include the lack of replication and SNP genotype imputation, which may affect the robustness of the results. The conclusion emphasizes the need for further exploration of the biological pathways involved in cardiac conduction abnormalities in PWH. The study was approved by an institutional review board and supported by various funding sources.

T o our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst and largest GWAS of
measuring genetic variants associated with ECG param-eters among Chinese PWH and HIV-negative controls.Nevertheless, several limitations warrant further consid-eration. First, replication study was not conducted given
difﬁculties in identifying additional studies of Chinese
PWH with ECG measures and genotype data, which mayreduce the robustness of our results to some extent.However, using the stringent Pvalue could reduce the
false discovery rate and candidate SNPs and genes werepresented for future validation. Second, no imputation ofSNP genotype was performed, as all genetic data wereavailable within one cohort and were obtained using asingle chip. However, all the association results were basedon the actual measurement of genetic variants, which maymake sure the authenticity of GWA analyses. Lastly, the
impact of higher ECG abnormality prevalence among
HIV-negative controls on genetic association analyses alsowarrants further exploration.
Conclusion
The present GWAS indicated a distinctive impact of hostgenome on quantitative ECG parameters among PWH,as well as signiﬁcant interaction effects between HIVinfection and genetic variants on ECG parameters.Different from HIV-negative controls, host genome
might inﬂuence the cardiac electrical activity by
interfering HIV viral infection, production, and latencyamong PWH. Better understanding of the biologicpathways and molecular genetics associated with cardiacconduction may offer insight into the pathogenesis ofconduction abnormalities among PWH.Acknowledgements

structure.summary: The partial document discusses a genome-wide association study (GWAS) that investigates the genetic variants associated with electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters in Chinese people living with HIV (PWH) and HIV-negative controls. It highlights the role of host genome in influencing cardiac electrical activity, particularly in the context of HIV infection, latency, and viral production. Key findings include the enrichment of specific genes related to ECG parameters, such as PR interval and QRS duration, and their association with cellular components like voltage-gated sodium channels. The study emphasizes the unique interactions between HIV infection and genetic variants affecting ECG parameters among PWH compared to HIV-negative individuals. Limitations of the study, such as the lack of replication and SNP genotype imputation, are acknowledged. The conclusion suggests that understanding the biological pathways involved may provide insights into conduction abnormalities in PWH. The document also includes acknowledgments for funding and contributions from various researchers involved in the study.

This further suggested that host genomemight affect the ECG parameters through inﬂuencingHIV viral activities.
Without the inﬂuence of HIV replication and integra-
tion, mapped genes among HIV-negative controls for PRinterval were enriched in the cellular component ofvoltage gated sodium channel complex and plasmamembrane protein complex. Voltage-gated sodiumchannels are key regulators of cellular excitability andstrongly involved in the generation of action potentials,heart contraction, and in the sensing of pain [52]. Incardiomyocytes, the rapid depolarization of the mem-brane potential is mediated by the cardiac voltage-gated
sodium channel, encoded by SCN5A which was involved
in all enriched pathway [52]. ITGA9 was involved in the
cellular component of plasma membrane proteincomplex and implicated in atrioventricular conductionand might mark a distal SCN5A regulatory element [53].
T o our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst and largest GWAS of
measuring genetic variants associated with ECG param-eters among Chinese PWH and HIV-negative controls.Nevertheless, several limitations warrant further consid-eration. First, replication study was not conducted given
difﬁculties in identifying additional studies of Chinese
PWH with ECG measures and genotype data, which mayreduce the robustness of our results to some extent.However, using the stringent Pvalue could reduce the
false discovery rate and candidate SNPs and genes werepresented for future validation. Second, no imputation ofSNP genotype was performed, as all genetic data wereavailable within one cohort and were obtained using asingle chip. However, all the association results were basedon the actual measurement of genetic variants, which maymake sure the authenticity of GWA analyses. Lastly, the
impact of higher ECG abnormality prevalence among
HIV-negative controls on genetic association analyses alsowarrants further exploration.
Conclusion
The present GWAS indicated a distinctive impact of hostgenome on quantitative ECG parameters among PWH,as well as signiﬁcant interaction effects between HIVinfection and genetic variants on ECG parameters.Different from HIV-negative controls, host genome
might inﬂuence the cardiac electrical activity by
interfering HIV viral infection, production, and latencyamong PWH. Better understanding of the biologicpathways and molecular genetics associated with cardiacconduction may offer insight into the pathogenesis ofconduction abnormalities among PWH.Acknowledgements
